interest: This document provides a revealing, micro-level glimpse into deteriorating Anglo-Japanese relations in the months immediately preceding the outbreak of the Pacific War in late 1941. It illustrates how mounting diplomatic friction translated into petty bureaucratic retaliation, specifically the weaponization of passport and transit visa controls against private citizens such as British commercial and banking figures in Japanese-occupied Manchuria. Furthermore, it highlights the stark contrast in Japanese treatment of British and American nationals in mid-1941, as demonstrated by the fact that the British banker's American wife obtained her visa without difficulty while her husband was blocked from a simple transfer between train and steamer at Dairen.
overview: This file contains diplomatic correspondence from June 1941 generated by the American Consulate General in Harbin, Manchuria, reporting on the Japanese Foreign Office's deliberate policy of obstructing visa issuance to British subjects. It consists of a cover despatch (No. 107) from American Consul Louis H. Gourley forwarding to the Department of State a copy of his confidential despatch No. 73 to American Ambassador Clarence E. Gauss in Peiping. Gourley details how Tokyo centralized and stalled visa approvals for British nationals in retaliation for restrictions placed on Japanese applicants throughout the British Empire, citing a candid admission by a Japanese consular official in Harbin during the case of a prominent British bank manager seeking a simple transit visa through Dairen en route to Shanghai.

subfiles.about: Cover despatch transmitting to the Department of State a copy of despatch No. 73 to the American Embassy in Peiping concerning Japanese visa obstruction against British subjects.
subfiles.from: Louis H. Gourley, American Consul at Harbin
subfiles.summary: American Consul Louis H. Gourley transmits to the Secretary of State quintuplicate copies of his confidential despatch No. 73 of June 19, 1941, originally sent to Ambassador Clarence E. Gauss in Peiping. The enclosed report details the Japanese Foreign Office's obstructive visa policy toward British subjects. The document was received and stamped by the State Department on August 2, 1941.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 107 from Gourley (Harbin) to Secretary of State enclosing despatch on Japanese visa policy

subfiles.about: Confidential report detailing the Japanese Foreign Office's retaliatory policy of obstructing visas for British subjects, illustrated by the case of a British banker transiting Dairen.
subfiles.from: Louis H. Gourley, American Consul at Harbin
subfiles.summary: Consul Gourley reports that the Japanese Foreign Office required all visa requests from British subjects to be referred directly to Tokyo, implementing an obstructive policy in retaliation for British visa restrictions on Japanese nationals throughout the British Empire. This retaliatory stance was openly confirmed by a Japanese consular officer in Harbin regarding the delayed application of a prominent British bank official transferring from Harbin to Shanghai, who required only a transit visa between the train station and steamer in Dairen. While the British banker's application was held up, his wife had promptly obtained a visa on her American passport two weeks prior. Copies were circulated to American diplomatic posts in Chungking, Mukden, Dairen, Tokyo, and Washington.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 73 from Gourley (Harbin) to Gauss (Peiping) on Japanese obstructive visa policy
subfiles.to: Clarence E. Gauss, American Ambassador at Peiping
